concepts.name: Tiered compilation, ReadyToRun and dynamic PGO
GitHub Actions OIDC federation to Azure

questions.prompt: `var report = await BuildReportAsync().WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));` Here `BuildReportAsync` takes no `CancellationToken` and runs for 30 seconds. What happens after 5 seconds?

choices.text: The await throws `TimeoutException`, and the report work carries on in the background
The await throws `TimeoutException`, and the runtime aborts the thread doing the report
The await throws `OperationCanceledException`, and the report task moves to `Canceled`
Nothing happens until 30 seconds, as `WaitAsync` only checks once the work has finished

questions.explanation: `WaitAsync` returns a new task that represents the wait: it faults with `TimeoutException` when the timeout passes, but it can't stop the original operation. Cancellation in .NET is cooperative, so the report keeps running, using resources, until it ends. To actually stop work, pass a `CancellationToken` (for example from a `CancellationTokenSource` with `CancelAfter`) that the operation observes.

sources.title: Task.WaitAsync Method (System.Threading.Tasks)
sources.claim: WaitAsync(TimeSpan) returns a Task representing the asynchronous wait, which completes when the original task completes or faults with a TimeoutException when the timeout expires.

sources.claim: Cancellation is cooperative and not forced on the listener; each listener must notice the request; a linked token source joins several tokens, and CancellationTokenSource objects, including linked ones, should be disposed.

questions.prompt: After each deploy, the first minute of requests to a .NET 8 API is slower than steady state, although it is published with `PublishReadyToRun=true`. Which explanation fits how the runtime compiles code?

choices.text: ReadyToRun turns the JIT off, so the slow minute is spent loading bigger DLLs
ReadyToRun code is less optimized, and tiering re-JITs hot methods over time
Dynamic PGO is off by default, so hot methods stay at tier 0 until enabled
Tiering is disabled with ReadyToRun, so methods are fully compiled on first call

questions.explanation: ReadyToRun cuts startup JIT work, but its precompiled code isn't as optimized as JIT output, so tiered compilation replaces commonly used methods with optimized JIT code, guided by dynamic PGO, which is on by default since .NET 8. Until hot methods reach that tier, the app runs slower than steady state. The JIT also still runs for code ReadyToRun can't precompile.

sources.title: ReadyToRun deployment overview - .NET
sources.claim: ReadyToRun reduces JIT work at startup but its code is not as highly optimized as JIT-produced code, so tiered compilation replaces commonly used ReadyToRun methods with JIT-generated ones; some code still needs the JIT.

sources.title: Compilation config settings - .NET
sources.claim: Tiered compilation's first tier uses quick JIT or loads ReadyToRun code and the second tier generates optimized code in the background; dynamic PGO works with tiered compilation using instrumentation put in place during tier 0.

sources.title: What's new in .NET 8 runtime
sources.claim: In .NET 8 dynamic profile-guided optimization is enabled by default and no longer needs a runtime configuration option.

questions.prompt: Your GitHub Actions workflow deploys to Azure with a client secret stored in repository secrets. How would you replace it with OpenID Connect, and how do you limit which workflows can use the Azure identity?

model_answer.summary: Trust GitHub's OIDC tokens through a federated credential on an Entra identity, let the job request a token and exchange it at login, and scope the trust with the subject claim.
key_points: Add a federated credential to an Entra app registration or user-assigned managed identity that trusts GitHub's OIDC issuer, and give that identity only the roles the deploy needs
Grant the job `permissions: id-token: write` and give `azure/login` the client ID, tenant ID and subscription ID, with no client secret
At login the job exchanges a short-lived GitHub token for an Entra access token, so nothing long-lived is stored
Scope the trust with the subject claim, such as `repo:org/repo:environment:production`, which must match exactly along with issuer and audience

questions.explanation: OIDC removes the stored secret and its rotation. The subject claim is the access control: trusting a specific repository and environment means a workflow in another repository, or a job without that environment, can't get an Azure token.

sources.title: OpenID Connect reference
sources.claim: The job must grant id-token: write to get an OIDC token; the subject claim is repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME when the job references an environment, and repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH only when it doesn't and the trigger isn't a pull request.

sources.title: Configuring OpenID Connect in Azure
sources.claim: Add a federated credential to the Entra ID application, grant id-token: write, and give azure/login the client ID, tenant ID and subscription ID, so no Azure credentials are stored as long-lived GitHub secrets.

sources.title: Workload Identity Federation - Microsoft Entra Workload ID
sources.claim: A federated identity credential on a user-assigned managed identity or app registration trusts an external IdP such as GitHub; the workload exchanges the external token for a Microsoft identity platform access token; issuer, subject and audience must match case-sensitively.

questions.prompt: An endpoint must give up on a slow downstream call after 2 seconds, and also stop if the request itself is aborted. How would you build this with cancellation tokens, and why isn't `WaitAsync` alone enough?

model_answer.summary: Link the request's token with a timeout token, pass the linked token to the downstream call, and dispose the source; `WaitAsync` only stops the wait, not the work.
key_points: Create a linked `CancellationTokenSource` from the request's token and call `CancelAfter(2 seconds)` on it
Pass the linked token to the downstream call, so the operation itself notices cancellation and stops
Dispose the `CancellationTokenSource` when done (with `using`), since timer-based sources hold timer resources
`WaitAsync` only stops waiting: cancellation is cooperative, so work that never sees a token keeps running

questions.explanation: A timeout that doesn't reach the operation leaves work running after the caller has given up, which under load piles up. A linked token gives the call one token that fires on either condition.

questions.prompt: What does dynamic profile-guided optimization (PGO) do in .NET 8 and later?

choices.text: Needs a training run at build time and stores the profile inside the binaries
Replaces tiered compilation, so each method is compiled once, fully optimized
Uses data from tier-0 instrumentation to optimize hot code when it is re-JITed
Is opt-in through `DOTNET_TieredPGO=1`, and only affects ReadyToRun framework code

questions.explanation: Dynamic PGO works with tiered compilation: instrumentation added at tier 0 records which types and paths are actually used, and the JIT uses it when it recompiles hot methods. It needs no training run, and since .NET 8 it is on by default (`DOTNET_TieredPGO=0` turns it off).

questions.prompt: A federated credential trusts subject `repo:contoso/api:ref:refs/heads/main`. You add `environment: production` to the deploy job on `main`, and `azure/login` starts failing. Why?

choices.text: Jobs with an environment can't get OIDC tokens, so a secret is needed
Environment protection rules remove `id-token: write` from the job
The token's audience becomes the environment name, so `aud` fails
The token's subject is now `repo:contoso/api:environment:production`

questions.explanation: When a job references an environment, GitHub puts the environment in the subject claim instead of the branch. Entra requires issuer, subject and audience to match the federated credential exactly, so the old `ref:refs/heads/main` credential no longer matches. Add a federated credential for the environment subject; it is also the tighter scope.

questions.prompt: You replace the client secret your GitHub Actions workflow uses to deploy to Azure with OpenID Connect and a federated credential on an Entra identity. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The job needs `permissions: id-token: write` to request GitHub's OIDC token
The job swaps GitHub's token for an Entra access token, so no secret is stored
A subject like `repo:org/app:environment:production` limits which jobs can log in
The federated credential matches the token's subject case-insensitively
Only a system-assigned managed identity can hold a federated identity credential

questions.explanation: A job must grant `id-token: write` to get a GitHub OIDC token. At login it sends that short-lived token to the Microsoft identity platform, which checks the federated credential and issues an access token, so no long-lived secret is stored. The subject claim is the access control: when a job references an environment its subject is `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME`, so trusting that subject keeps other repositories and jobs out. Issuer, subject and audience must match case-sensitively, and the credential goes on an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity.

sources.title: OpenID Connect reference
sources.claim: The job must grant id-token: write to request an OIDC token; when the job references an environment the subject claim is repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME.

sources.title: Workload Identity Federation - Microsoft Entra Workload ID
sources.claim: A federated identity credential on a user-assigned managed identity or app registration trusts an external IdP such as GitHub; the workload exchanges the external token for a Microsoft identity platform access token without managing secrets; issuer, subject and audience must match case-sensitively.

questions.prompt: An endpoint must give up on a slow downstream call after 2 seconds, and also stop if the request itself is aborted. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A linked token source can join the request's token with a timeout
The downstream call stops only if it is passed the token and observes it
Dispose the linked `CancellationTokenSource` once the call finishes
`WaitAsync(TimeSpan)` cancels the original task when the timeout expires
Cancelling a token forcibly aborts the thread still running the operation

questions.explanation: `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource` joins the request's token with your own, and `CancelAfter` on it adds the timeout, so one token fires on either condition. Cancellation is cooperative: the downstream call stops only if it receives the token and notices it, and nothing is aborted by force. Linked token sources must be disposed, and undisposed timeout sources put pressure on the timer queue. `WaitAsync` only gives you a task for the wait, which faults with `TimeoutException`; the original work keeps running.

sources.title: Cancellation in Managed Threads - .NET
sources.claim: Cancellation is cooperative and not forced on the listener, which must notice the request; a linked token source joins several tokens into one, and CancellationTokenSource objects, including linked ones, must be disposed.

sources.title: Task.WaitAsync Method (System.Threading.Tasks)
sources.claim: WaitAsync(TimeSpan) returns a task representing the asynchronous wait, which completes when the original task completes or is faulted with a TimeoutException when the timeout expires.

sources.title: AspNetCoreDiagnosticScenarios: AsyncGuidance.md
sources.claim: Always dispose CancellationTokenSource objects used for timeouts, since undisposed ones put pressure on the timer queue; prefer Task.WaitAsync to stop waiting on operations that can't be cancelled.
